USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep the G20 90-day truce and press the Beijing talks without new tariff hikes, rollbacks, or purchase-only deals. Use the scheduled March List 3 increase (10% to 25% on ~$200B) as leverage for enforceable IP, tech-transfer, and market-access commitments, while accepting limited Chinese agricultural/energy purchases only as a down payment, not the deal. Do not politicize the Meng extradition or add firms to the entity list during this window; a fresh escalation now would likely draw more farm-sector retaliation and blow up the only live negotiating track.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is moderately elevated, not existential. Combined Section 301 coverage is already ~$250B (Lists 1–3), and China has matched on ~$50B plus 5–10% on ~$60B more, with soybeans, autos, and aircraft explicitly targeted. U.S. goods exports to China have fallen sharply (EXPCH from $9.28B in Aug 2018 to $7.11B in Jan 2019, about −23%), and soybean sales to China collapsed after the July 25% duty—Jan–Oct 2018 exports to China were ~63% below 2017, with prices down roughly $2/bu. That is a real hit to a politically sensitive export sector, not a free lunch. Consumer sentiment dropped to 91.2 in January from 98.3 in December and VIX spiked to 36 on Dec 24 before easing to ~20, so financial and household conditions have tightened even if industrial production is only slightly softer. This is below the +0.5 “material GDP drag” anchor because the U.S. still has unused leverage (the March 1/2 List 3 hike), China is offering purchases and has suspended extra auto tariffs, and Chinese IP/reserves are not collapsing. Action should stay at hold/negotiate: mid-level talks just resumed in Beijing on Jan 7 with purchases on the table and structural issues still open; the May 2018 “trade war on hold” statement collapsed within days when Washington proceeded with 301, so premature rollback would repeat that error, while hiking now would violate the Dec 1 Trump–Xi pause and likely trigger further ag retaliation before senior talks. The Meng arrest and the Kovrig/Spavor detentions raise the cost of mixing law-enforcement with tariffs; keep them compartmentalized and extract the structural concessions the 301 record was built to get.
key_factors: G20 90-day pause keeps List 3 at 10% with a March hike still live as leverage
Jan 7 Beijing working-level talks: China discussing purchases; IP/tech-transfer/state-support issues unresolved
U.S. farm-belt exposure: soybean market largely shut, EXPCH down ~23% since August
Financial/household stress (UMCSENT 91.2, Dec VIX spike) raises the cost of immediate re-escalation
Meng/Huawei overlay and Canadian detainee retaliation risk contaminating the trade track if mixed
Prior May 2018 truce collapsed when the U.S. proceeded with 301 — do not concede the tariff clock for a purchases-only deal

sources_cited.excerpt: G20 Buenos Aires dinner: Trump and Xi agree to a 90-day negotiation window. Planned Jan 1, 2019 hike of List 3 from 10% to 25% is suspended (tariffs remain at 10%). Same day: Canada arrests Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou.
Trade talks resume in Beijing (working / mid-level). China discusses increased purchases of US goods; structural issues remain open.
List 3 takes effect at 10%. China imposes retaliatory tariffs (5–10%) on ~$60B of US goods. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.
US and China release joint statement after talks: China agrees to "significantly increase" purchases of US goods and services. Mnuchin says trade war is "on hold."
China detains Canadians Michael Kovrig and Michael Spavor (widely viewed as retaliation for the Meng arrest; Beijing denies linkage).
U.S. exports of goods to mainland China fell from $9,278M (2018-08) to $7,105M (2019-01), change_pct about -23.4%.
University of Michigan consumer sentiment fell from 98.3 (2018-12) to 91.2 (2019-01).
VIX closed at 36.07 on 2018-12-24 and was still 19.98 on 2019-01-09, well above mid-summer teens.
Talks began ahead of a tariff increase from 10% to 25% on $200B scheduled for March 2; mid-level only, Lighthizer absent; U.S. wants structural changes on IP, tech transfer, and other barriers.
U.S. soybean exports to China for January–October 2018 were 63% lower than the same period in 2017; China levied 25% retaliatory tariffs on U.S. soybeans.
